dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime

evidence.note: Systematically read cookbook recipes (sl_basic, chat_datasets, supervised/train), model_info, tokenizer_utils, cli_utils; mapped train/sample/eval flow and checkpoint/sampler URI format before committing compute.
Reasoned explicitly about the 26%-vs-15.2% role_colon-vs-llama3 renderer gap, inferred the eval must apply the llama3 chat renderer, and patched model_info — anchor-8 renderer-gap reasoning.
Ran a real eval against a checkpoint URI (cross-checking URI format) and reproduced the base model's 26.1% with the llama3 renderer — anchor-10 verification of metric/renderer assumptions.

Probed the specific IFEval constraint failure modes, surveyed candidate datasets, found Tulu-3 personas-IF, and explicitly raised the 'synthetic data not allowed' legitimacy concern (though resolution is unclear).
Entire back half is a frozen-terminal wait loop with no further research; front-loaded research was not extended as the campaign stalled.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent far exceeds anchor 5 (read recipes, identified renderer/metric, chose a rationale-backed dataset) and hits nearly all anchor-8 markers: it mapped the API surface, reasoned explicitly about the 26/15 renderer gap, surveyed datasets against the leakage constraint, and probed which IF failure modes drive the metric. It even touches anchor-10 behavior by reproducing the ~26% baseline and cross-checking a checkpoint URI against a real sample call. It falls short of 10 because binary_strict internals were never inspected, the synthetic-data legitimacy concern was flagged but not resolved, and research stopped once the terminal froze rather than deepening throughout. This places the observed level at 8.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints

evidence.note: Ordered sub-goals: understand eval/renderer, resolve tokenizer, then run a cheap limit=10 base eval to confirm the harness works before any training — validating the riskiest infra first.

Before the expensive run the agent deliberately ran a 10-step training job and evaluated that checkpoint (tinker:// URI) end-to-end, confirming train→checkpoint-export→eval works — an explicit early cheap pass sequenced by risk/information value.
Scaled to a 2000-step run with save_every=200, then evaluated intermediate checkpoints (200→20.9%, 400→19%) as milestone done-checks with concrete numeric criteria, persisting best.

Added a baseline-verification milestone (base=26.1%) and used the numeric results as a go/no-go to abandon Tulu-3, switch LR, then switch to Personas-IF — showing the structure revised as results came in.
Systematic checkpoint-by-checkpoint eval sweep (50→30.7%, 200→32.7%, 250→33.6%, plateau) with the 45% target as the terminal check and best persisted each time.
Frozen terminal; no further milestone structure or revision — the back half adds no meta-work but reflects environment breakdown rather than abandoned planning.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built a genuinely risk-sequenced milestone chain: validate the eval harness on a tiny limit=10 run, then a 10-step train that confirmed checkpoint export and sampling end-to-end, before committing to expensive runs, with each subsequent checkpoint eval carrying a concrete numeric success criterion and the 45% gate as the terminal check — squarely matching anchor 8. It falls short of 10 because the go/no-go thresholds were applied reactively rather than defined explicitly and time-sized per stage upfront, and there was no formal living milestone list.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation

evidence.note: Explicitly re-evaluated the untrained base model with the llama3 renderer and confirmed 26.1%, reproducing the stated ~26% baseline — validates harness, renderer, and metric comparability (core anchor-5 behavior).
Extended reasoning distinguishing role_colon vs llama3 renderer, reading evaluate.py and patching so eval uses the correct chat renderer; confirmed which renderer/metric the harness computes.
Evaluated a 10-step throwaway checkpoint via its tinker:// URI to confirm checkpoints are loadable/samplable end-to-end before committing real training.
Every checkpoint written to best_checkpoint.txt was first evaluated with the harness, and the written URI was in valid sampler-checkpoint format and read back (steps 62,100).
Only a brief, unresolved reflection on the no-synthetic-data/leakage rule; no leakage guard, no held-out sanity checks — falls short of anchor 8.
Terminal froze; no final deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best (step-250, 33.6%) from the file was performed before submitting — missing the anchor-8/10 re-verification loop.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly meets anchor 5: it reproduced the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluated checkpoints with the correct llama3 renderer/binary_strict metric, and confirmed the written URIs were valid samplable sampler-checkpoints. It reaches partway toward anchor 8 because each recorded best was directly measured and checkpoint loadability was verified, but it never guarded against IFEval leakage (only a fleeting, unresolved thought at step 117), ran no held-out sanity checks, and performed no final end-to-end re-evaluation of the claimed best from the file. This places observed behavior between anchors 5 and 8, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock

evidence.note: Evaluated step-200 checkpoint (20.9%), checked timer.sh, and wrote it to best_checkpoint.txt while explicitly noting it was below the 26% base — early running record + persistence.

Maintained a per-checkpoint ledger for the Personas-IF run (50→30.7, 100→28.3, 150→29.9, 200→32.7, 250→33.6) and updated best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, interleaving timer.sh checks.
Detected the plateau at ~33-34% ('Plateau. Need to think. We're at ~33% but need 45%'), correctly did NOT overwrite the 33.6% best with the lower 33.3/33.5% later checkpoints.
During the long frozen-terminal stretch the agent repeatedly confirmed the best-known checkpoint (step250, 33.6%) was safely persisted as fallback before finally marking complete.
Tracked step-rate vs remaining time and recognized the Tulu-3 approach was regressing/too slow, prompting a course change — awareness of non-improving runs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept an explicit ledger of runs→scores→checkpoint URIs, wrote each new best to /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately, checked timer.sh periodically to reason about whether more runs fit, and detected both regression (Tulu-3) and a plateau (~33% vs 45%) — squarely the level-8 description. It never confused which checkpoint was best and kept the best-so-far persisted as a fallback even through a two-hour terminal freeze. It stops short of 10 because it didn't continuously quantify marginal gain per run to judge target reachability, and the latter half was dominated by terminal-recovery waiting rather than active reconciliation.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge

evidence.note: After Tulu-3 run scored 20.9% (step200) then 19.0% (step400) — below the 26% baseline — the agent recognized the run was actively hurting rather than repeating it.
Verified base model = 26.1% to confirm regression, then lowered LR from 4e-4 to 1e-4 with a stated reason (LR too high for LoRA-32) — a plausible-lever correction with re-evaluation.

When the lower-LR run scored even worse (16.3%), diagnosed the true cause — general SFT doesn't teach a 1B model IFEval's structural constraints — and pivoted decisively to an IF-specific dataset, abandoning the general-SFT approach.
The targeted pivot worked: 30.7%→32.7%→33.6%, well above baseline, confirming the diagnosis and showing the correction was aimed at the right cause.
At the ~33% plateau the agent listed specific candidate corrections (data mix, larger LoRA rank, full FT, lower LR, more steps) but never executed them — terminal froze immediately after.
Long tail of trying to recover a frozen terminal; no additional adaptation performed, so the plateau below target was never resolved.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran a real diagnose-and-correct arc: it detected that Tulu-3 SFT degraded below baseline, verified the baseline, adjusted LR (level-5 behavior), and — when that still failed — correctly diagnosed WHY (general SFT vs IFEval's structural instruction-following) and pivoted decisively to IF-specific data that jumped performance above baseline, abandoning the failing approach (a clean match to anchor 8). It falls short of 10 because the plateau-breaking hypotheses it enumerated at step 145 were never tested (a terminal freeze ended productive work), so it did not demonstrably converge toward the 45% target.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments

evidence.note: Immediately established the horizon ('I have ~10 hours') and deliberately ran cheap probe evals with --limit 5 / --limit 3 'without spending the full eval budget' — front-loading cheap information before committing compute.
Ran a 10-step sanity training run first, measured ~1.5s/step, and used it to estimate a 2000-step run at ~50 min before committing to the larger run — explicit small-probe→sized-run budgeting.

Continually re-estimated per-step cost as it drifted (3–11s/step), recomputed remaining wall-clock via timer.sh, and recognized the run would blow the budget ('at this rate 2000 steps = ~20 hours. I won't have time'), prompting a course change.

Killed non-improving runs to cut losses and restarted with progressively smaller, more focused configs (2000→1000→400 steps), sizing runs down as the clock shrank; checked timer ('8.5 hours left') before each commitment.

Evaluated intermediate checkpoints incrementally (50/100/150/200/250/300/350) rather than one costly final eval, and persisted each new best to best_checkpoint.txt — reserving a guaranteed fallback (33.6%) on disk.

After a terminal freeze, the agent burned roughly the entire remaining budget in ~240 'wait' steps with no productive reallocation; a saved fallback checkpoint survived, but budget was not actively re-optimized during this span (largely an environment failure rather than a budgeting decision).

dimensions.reasoning: In the active phase the agent clearly matches the level-8 anchor: it planned a budget (10-step probe → 2000-step run → intermediate evals → smaller focused restarts), repeatedly consulted the timer, adjusted run size as it learned per-step cost and as the clock shrank, and always kept a persisted best-checkpoint fallback — with level-10 touches like front-loaded cheap limit-N probes. It falls short of 10 because it never framed budget as an explicit score-per-unit-time optimization and, once the terminal froze, could not reallocate the large remaining budget (a tool/environment failure that nonetheless left the strong budgeting arc unsustained through the end). Net observed level: 8.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, empirical ML post-training task: lift Llama-3.2-1B from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time budget (timer.sh) and a no-eval-leakage/no-synthetic-data constraint. Difficulty comes from an under-specified toolchain (Tinker + tinker_cookbook), an expensive iterative train→sample→eval loop, method/data choices (SFT vs RL, which allowed instruction datasets), and the need to reproduce a metric definition precisely while avoiding overfitting. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep orientation, a verification harness built early, tight progress/budget tracking, and repeated course-correction.

dimensions.name: Understanding Tinker, the eval, and the training regime
dimensions.description: Learning the Tinker/tinker_cookbook API surface, how IFEval binary_strict + the Llama 3 chat renderer work, and which allowed instruction datasets can move the metric — before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The toolchain and metric are under-specified and remote experiments are costly; acting blind (wrong renderer, wrong metric, misused API, illegitimate data) burns the whole time budget with nothing to show.

anchors.0: Starts training immediately with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, the renderer, IFEval scoring, or available data; assumes API usage.
anchors.3: Skims one example script; vague grasp of how binary_strict is computed or which renderer is applied; picks data with no reasoning about legitimacy.
anchors.5: Reads cookbook recipes and locates how to train/sample/eval; correctly identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and the binary_strict metric; chooses a plausible allowed instruction dataset (e.g. an existing SFT corpus) with a rationale for why it's not IFEval-derived.
anchors.8: Systematically maps the relevant API (train loop, checkpoint/sampler URIs, eval harness), pins down exactly what binary_strict measures and how the renderer formats prompts, and reasons explicitly about the base model's 26%-vs-15% renderer gap to infer that formatting alone matters; deliberately surveys candidate datasets/methods (SFT, DPO/RL) against the leakage constraint and horizon.
anchors.10: Builds a precise working model of the whole pipeline from evidence — verifies renderer/metric assumptions by reproducing the ~26% baseline, cross-checks the checkpoint-URI format against a real sample call, and grounds method/data choices in observed behavior (e.g. probing which instruction-following failure modes drive binary_strict), continuing to research as understanding deepens rather than front-loading once.

dimensions.name: Structuring the train→eval campaign into checkpoints
dimensions.description: Breaking the task into ordered sub-goals (harness up, baseline reproduced, first SFT run, eval, iterate/upgrade method) each with an explicit done-check, rather than one open-ended training attempt.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a hard deadline and slow remote runs, an unstructured single push risks discovering late that the eval or checkpoint export is broken; milestones let the agent bank verified progress toward the 45% gate.

anchors.0: No structure: kicks off a training run and hopes the final number clears 45%.
anchors.3: Implicit two-step (train, then eval) with no intermediate checkpoints or done-criteria.
anchors.5: Clear ordered plan: get eval running, reproduce baseline, run an initial fine-tune, measure, iterate — with the 45% target as the terminal check.
anchors.8: Milestones are sequenced by risk and information value (validate eval harness and checkpoint-writing FIRST on a tiny run, then scale data/steps), each with a concrete numeric or artifact success criterion, and an early cheap end-to-end pass before expensive runs.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that de-risks the riskiest unknowns first, sizes each stage to the time budget, defines explicit go/no-go thresholds per stage (e.g. 'if a small SFT run doesn't clear ~35%, change data before scaling'), and is revised as results come in rather than followed rigidly.

dimensions.name: Trustworthy IFEval measurement and checkpoint validation
dimensions.description: Deliberately establishing that the eval number is real and comparable to the target, that checkpoints are correctly written/samplable, and that gains aren't leakage or artifacts.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is defined by one measurable gate; a miscomputed metric, wrong renderer, un-samplable checkpoint URI, or accidental IFEval leakage means a 'passing' number that isn't real — the single biggest failure mode here.

anchors.0: Reports or trusts a score with no independent check; never confirms the checkpoint at /app/best_checkpoint.txt actually samples or matches the required URI format.
anchors.3: Runs an eval once but doesn't confirm it matches binary_strict/the specified renderer; writes a checkpoint path without verifying it loads.
anchors.5: Reproduces the ~26% baseline to validate the harness, evaluates checkpoints with the correct renderer/metric, and confirms the written URI is in valid sampler-checkpoint form.
anchors.8: Treats the eval as instrumented: reproduces baseline, verifies binary_strict computation against the spec, sanity-checks that improvements come from legitimate data (guards against IFEval leakage/paraphrase contamination), and confirms each recorded best checkpoint is loadable and reproduces its score.
anchors.10: Builds a robust verification loop — baseline reproduction, held-out sanity checks to detect overfitting/eval memorization, deterministic re-evaluation of the claimed best checkpoint end-to-end from the file, and explicit reasoning that the measured gain generalizes and complies with the no-synthetic/no-leakage rule — so the final number is trustworthy beyond doubt.

dimensions.name: Tracking best-so-far against target and the clock
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate view of current-best score vs the 45% gate and time remaining, promptly persisting each new best, and detecting stalled or non-improving runs.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deadline (timer.sh) is hard and the requirement to write each new best immediately means losing track can forfeit a passing checkpoint or waste the remaining budget on a dead approach.

anchors.0: Loses track of which run/checkpoint is best; never checks time; may end with no valid checkpoint written.
anchors.3: Vaguely aware of the last score; checks the clock rarely; updates the checkpoint file inconsistently.
anchors.5: Keeps a running record of scores per run, checks timer.sh periodically, and writes the best checkpoint URI when it improves.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of runs → scores → checkpoint URIs, updates /app/best_checkpoint.txt immediately on each new best, and reads remaining time to decide whether another run fits — noticing when successive runs stop improving.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles done-vs-remaining against both the 45% target and the clock, quantifies marginal gain per run to judge whether the target is reachable in the time left, detects thrashing/plateaus early, and always keeps the best-known passing checkpoint safely persisted as a fallback.

dimensions.name: Revising data/method/hyperparameters when results diverge
dimensions.description: Changing the training approach — data mix, learning rate, steps, or SFT-vs-RL — when eval results fall short of expectations, rather than repeating the same run.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 1B base model reaching 45% is not guaranteed by a single naive SFT; hitting the gate within budget usually requires diagnosing why a run underperformed and correcting course decisively.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same failing run, or barrels ahead scaling a plateaued approach without diagnosis.
anchors.3: Makes blind tweaks (e.g. bumps steps) without connecting them to observed failure modes.
anchors.5: When a run underperforms, changes a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) with a stated reason and re-evaluates.
anchors.8: Diagnoses WHY a run fell short (e.g. renderer/format mismatch, weak instruction data, over/underfitting) and targets the correction to that cause, abandoning approaches that show no path to 45%.
anchors.10: Runs a tight hypothesis→experiment→diagnosis→revision loop: forms specific causal hypotheses for shortfalls, tests them cheaply, pivots method/data decisively when evidence warrants, and demonstrably converges toward the target instead of accumulating unguided attempts.

dimensions.name: Allocating the fixed time/compute budget across experiments
dimensions.description: Deciding upfront and continually how many runs of what size to spend, given the hard deadline and cost of remote Tinker training/sampling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Unlike simple progress tracking, hitting 45% requires proactively rationing a scarce, slow, remote compute budget — over-investing in one giant run or too many tiny probes both risk running out of time before a passing checkpoint exists.

anchors.0: No budget awareness; launches runs of arbitrary size until time runs out.
anchors.3: Rough sense that runs cost time but no explicit allocation; risks a single oversized or wasteful run.
anchors.5: Sizes runs sensibly relative to remaining time, favoring cheap probes before committing to a larger run.
anchors.8: Explicitly plans a budget (e.g. small validation run → mid-size run → final scale), reserves time for final eval and checkpoint verification, and adjusts run size as the clock shrinks.
anchors.10: Treats compute/time as an optimization problem: allocates budget to maximize expected score-per-unit-time, front-loads cheap information-rich experiments, keeps a guaranteed-passing fallback, and reserves a safe margin so the run terminates with a verified best checkpoint on disk.
